articles.title: gRPC has no [Authorize] seam: enforcing Keyright entitlements with a server-side Interceptor
articles.excerpt: An ASP.NET Core Web API gives you a tidy seam for license checks: an authorization policy, an [Authorize(Policy = "ent:export")] attribute, and the request is rejected before your action runs. A gRPC…
articles.body: An ASP.NET Core Web API gives you a tidy seam for license checks: an authorization policy, an [Authorize(Policy = "ent:export")] attribute, and the request is rejected before your action runs. A gRPC service has none of that. There is no controller, no action filter pipeline, no attribute that the framework evaluates per call. If you try to scatter if (license.HasEntitlement("export")) through your service methods you are back to the thing the HTTP authorization pipeline was built to replace — a check you have to remember to write in every method, where forgetting one ships a feature unlicensed. gRPC does have one seam that sees every call, though, and it is the right place to put this: the server-side Interceptor .

articles.title: Making PDFs tamper-evident in the browser with SHA-256 (and why we hash the sealed file, not the original)
articles.excerpt: AI has made it trivial to edit an invoice, a quote or a contract so cleanly that nobody can spot the change by eye. A PDF has no memory: the file name, the date and the layout all look the same after…
articles.body: AI has made it trivial to edit an invoice, a quote or a contract so cleanly that nobody can spot the change by eye. A PDF has no memory: the file name, the date and the layout all look the same after someone changes "1,800 €" to "4,800 €". So instead of trying to detect a forgery by how it looks, we built TRAMPTO to prove that a document hasn't changed, with plain math. This post walks through how it works, the one design decision that bit us, and what this approach does not prove. The idea in one line Compute a SHA-256 fingerprint of the document, register it, and give the recipient a link where they can recompute it themselves. Change one byte and the fingerprint no longer matches. Hashing in the browser with Web Crypto No libraries needed.

articles.title: How Glass follows type forwarding and the ExportedType table
articles.excerpt: Few pieces of .NET metadata cause as much confusion as the type forwarder. You open an old assembly — mscorlib, say, or a netstandard facade — ask your tools for System.ValueTuple, and the type is lis…
articles.body: Few pieces of .NET metadata cause as much confusion as the type forwarder. You open an old assembly — mscorlib , say, or a netstandard facade — ask your tools for System.ValueTuple , and the type is listed but has no code. It is not a stub the compiler forgot to fill in. It is a forwarder: a one-line signpost that says the type physically lives somewhere else now. A decompiler that does not understand that will show you an empty class, or an unresolved reference, and either way it has failed at its one job. This is about how Glass.NET handles the case correctly — where the forward lives in metadata, how Glass follows it (even across a chain), what it does when the target is nowhere to be found, and how it re-emits the forward when you decompile the forwarding assembly itself.

articles.title: Building a Name Numerology Calculator in Python: Chaldean vs Pythagorean, With Tests
articles.excerpt: Name numerology turns the letters of a name into numbers. Two letter-value systems dominate: Pythagorean (1–9 repeating) and Chaldean (1–8, based on sound vibration). The same name gives different tot…
articles.body: Name numerology turns the letters of a name into numbers. Two letter-value systems dominate: Pythagorean (1–9 repeating) and Chaldean (1–8, based on sound vibration). The same name gives different totals under each system, which is exactly what makes this a good small calculator project — the rules are simple, the edge cases are real, and the arithmetic is easy to test. This post builds a dependency-free Python calculator for the three classic numbers — Destiny (all letters), Soul Urge (vowels only), Personality (consonants only) — and tests it against hand-checked examples.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 13, 1971: NASA's Mariner 9 becomes 1st spacecraft to orbit Mars, revealing close looks at the Martian surface
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 13, 1971, Mariner 9 became the first spacecraft to orbit Mars. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 13, 1971, Mariner 9 became the first spacecraft to orbit Mars. At the time, scientists didn't know much about the Red Planet. NASA had several Mars flybys before Mariner 9 . Those flybys showed that Mars had a cratered surface , so some scientists thought that Mars looked just like the moon. Then Mariner 9 blew blew their minds. When Mariner 9 got to Mars , it arrived in the middle of a dust storm. It saw some tall structures sticking through the clouds. When the dust settled, images from Mariner 9 revealed that these structures were the tops of huge volcanoes. One volcano, Olympus Mons , is the tallest in the solar system. Mariner 9 also spotted an enormous canyon called Valles Marineris . This canyon is five times longer than the Grand Canyon in Arizona.

articles.body: This year marks a rather auspicious anniversary for meteor watchers. Sixty years ago , one of the most stupendous Leonid meteor displays lit up the predawn skies over the central and western U.S. So, what will the 2026 Leonids bring us? And what might they bring in the years to come? The Leonid meteor shower is one of the most celebrated of the year's annual displays of "shooting stars." The mere mention of the Leonids usually elicits mental images of a sky filled with shooting stars pouring down through the sky like rain. Such meteor storms have indeed occurred with the Leonids, such as in 1833 and 1966 when meteor rates of tens of thousands per hour were observed.

articles.body: In many of the biggest science fiction franchises, conversing with alien races is an absolute doddle. articles.title: Think you have good eyesight? Try counting the stars in the Pleiades tonight
articles.excerpt: Every November, I give myself a completely unscientific eyesight test using one of my favorite sights in the night sky — the Pleiades. How many stars can you see?
articles.body: Every autumn, I conduct an eyesight test that no reputable optometrist would understand. I go outside, find the Pleiades and count how many stars I can see. Usually I start confidently. One, two, three, four, five. Then things become contentious. Is that another star? Did I actually see it, or did I decide I ought to see it because I know it's there? I look away, look back and begin again. This is not, I should emphasize, a meaningful test of eye health. What it tests, rather, is how badly I've prepared for looking at the night sky. The Pleiades sit roughly 444 light-years away in Taurus and are right now becoming extremely convenient in the evening sky. You don't need a telescope to find them. You don't even need binoculars.

articles.title: Windows 0-day dropped by disgruntled researcher hands hackers System rights
articles.excerpt: "SignDrop" exploit lets local users gain all-powerful System rights.
articles.body: Nightmare Eclipse, the pseudonym of a researcher with an ongoing, very public beef with Microsoft, has dropped yet another Windows zero-day. On Tuesday, Nightmare Eclipse disclosed SignDrop, a vulnerability that gives local users full System rights on some versions of Windows. The vulnerability resides in the Common Log File System , which Microsoft describes as a “general-purpose logging service used by software clients running in user-mode or kernel-mode.” By forcing a privileged process such as Windows Defender to open a crafted CLFS container, an attacker with ordinary user rights can abuse the privileged file creation to elevate privileges to System. Turning a Windows defense against itself The attack exploits the interaction of CLFS, Windows Defender, and Windows file permissions.
